summary: Analyzes the privacy issues that come from using the DNS, such as what queries reveal about users and who can see them. It describes the situation at the time and does not prescribe solutions. It was replaced by RFC 9076.

eli5.summary: Every time you look up a website's address, you ask a question out loud. This explains who can overhear those questions and what they learn. It was replaced by RFC 9076.

subtitle: Understanding what your DNS queries reveal about you

tldr.problem: Nearly every internet activity starts with a DNS query that reveals what website or service a user is trying to access, but these queries are typically sent unencrypted and can be observed by network operators, ISPs, and other eavesdroppers.
tldr.mechanism: This document analyzes the different ways DNS queries leak privacy information, including what data is exposed, who can see it, how it can be collected and analyzed, and what inferences attackers can make from the patterns.
tldr.outcome: This informational document does not prescribe solutions but establishes that DNS privacy is a significant concern. It was replaced by RFC 9076 with updated analysis.

sections.title: How DNS Works and Why It Matters
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) is one of the most important but misunderstood parts of internet infrastructure. Almost every internet activity starts with a DNS query: when you type a URL into your browser, it asks a DNS server to translate the domain name (such as www.example.com) into an IP address so the connection can be made.

The query travels through several servers: your computer sends it to a recursive resolver (usually operated by your ISP or a public service), which then queries root name servers and authoritative name servers to find the answer. Unlike most other internet communications, the query stays the same at each step—the resolver asks the root servers the full question about www.example.com rather than just asking who handles .com.

This structure means that many parties see not just metadata, but the actual names of the resources you are trying to access.
sections.eli5: When you type a website address in your browser, your computer asks a helper to turn the name into a number. That helper asks other helpers, and they all see the full question about what you want.

sections.title: What DNS Queries Reveal
sections.content:
A DNS query contains two pieces of particularly sensitive information. The query name (QNAME) is the domain name you are asking about—if you query for mail.example.com, everyone seeing that query knows you are trying to access email at that domain. This is highly revealing: looking up a domain for a sensitive organization exposes your interest in it, even if the actual website traffic is encrypted.

The second is your source IP address. For queries from your computer to your ISP's resolver, this is your machine's address, which directly identifies you or a small group of people on your network. Even for queries to authoritative servers, techniques like EDNS Client Subnet can reveal your location or subnet to the domain operator.

The RFC notes that web browsers also make secondary and tertiary DNS requests beyond what the user directly requests: queries for stylesheets, images, scripts, and tracking services embedded in pages all leak information about what content the page contains, not just what page you visited.
sections.eli5: When you ask for a website, whoever hears the question learns exactly what site you want, and they can see your address so they know it was you who asked.

sections.title: Who Can See Your Queries
sections.content:
DNS queries can be observed at multiple points. On the wire between your computer and your ISP's resolver, an eavesdropper can intercept everything unencrypted. Between the ISP's resolver and the authoritative name servers, the attack surface varies—it could be limited to a corporate network, or span the entire internet if you use a public DNS service.

The recursive resolvers themselves (typically run by ISPs or services like Google Public DNS) see all your traffic because caching is typically done only at this level. The RFC emphasizes that your recursive resolver knows a lot about you. It collects all your queries, can store this data long-term, and may share it with third parties for research, security analysis, or surveillance programs.

Authoritative name servers see fewer queries because of caching, but they may see enough to identify patterns. They also may be operated by third parties in different countries under different legal frameworks. Additionally, rogue servers—whether through DHCP hijacking, malware, or transparent proxying—can intercept and observe traffic intended for legitimate resolvers.
sections.eli5: Your ISP can see every question you ask. Big public DNS services see everything too. Domain owners see some questions. And hackers can hijack your queries and watch them.

sections.title: Extracting Intelligence from Query Patterns
sections.content:
Query patterns themselves are revealing. Research shows that users can be re-identified purely from their DNS query patterns: if an observer knows your identity and watches your queries for a time, they can recognize the same patterns later even if you use a different IP address or location. One study found that 73% of day-to-day query patterns could be correctly re-linked to the same user.

Analysis techniques from security research can detect malware infections by identifying unusual DNS behavior. Passive DNS systems collect and store DNS responses (sometimes including client IP addresses), allowing reconstruction of an entire zone's history. The RFC cites the NSA's MORECOWBELL program as a real-world example of surveillance exploiting DNS's lack of privacy protections.

Traffic analysis can also infer information beyond the names queried: the length of query names, the timing of requests, and the sequence of lookups can all leak information about what applications are running, what the user is doing, or even which country they are in.
sections.eli5: Someone watching your questions can figure out who you are by recognizing your patterns. They can also tell what software you use or if your computer has a virus, just by watching the questions you ask.

sections.title: The Legal Landscape
sections.content:
The RFC notes that there are currently no specific privacy laws governing DNS data in most countries. Interpreting general privacy regulations (such as the EU's data protection directive) in the context of DNS query data is complex and there are few legal precedents. This legal ambiguity compounds the technical privacy risks: even where laws might theoretically protect query data, enforcement is unclear and varies by jurisdiction.

This uncertainty is particularly important given that domain operators may host their nameservers in countries different from the domain's registration country, potentially subjecting DNS data to different legal regimes.
sections.eli5: Different countries have different privacy rules, and it is not clear how those rules apply to DNS questions.
